title: Blood glucose: insulin and the oral antidiabetic drugs
ariaLabel: Schematic of what sets blood glucose: glucose from a meal and from the liver raise it, and glucose reabsorbed by the kidney returns to it; insulin release and tissue uptake lower it, and glucose lost in the urine lowers it too. Sulfonylureas and incretin drugs raise insulin release, thiazolidinediones raise insulin action, metformin lowers liver output and a little insulin resistance, and SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption so more is lost in the urine.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or glucose value is shown or implied.

drugs.label: DPP-4 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist type

blockInfo: A drug of the chosen class blocking this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape): less passes here.
enhanceInfo: A drug of the chosen class increasing this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape): more passes here.

nodes.label: Glucose from a meal
nodes.info: Glucose absorbed from food. The slider sets how much arrives.

nodes.label: Liver glucose output
nodes.info: The liver releases glucose between meals and during fasting, and does not switch off fully in type 2 diabetes. Insulin normally restrains it; glucagon drives it.

nodes.label: Blood glucose
nodes.info: Blood glucose: raised by food and by the liver, lowered by uptake into muscle and fat (and, above the renal threshold, by loss in the urine). The slider and the drug choice change the balance.

nodes.label: Insulin released
nodes.info: Insulin: released by pancreatic beta cells as glucose rises. Sulfonylureas and incretin-based drugs raise its release.

nodes.label: Tissue uptake
nodes.info: Insulin moves GLUT4 transporters to the surface of muscle and fat cells so glucose can enter. Resistance of this step is the heart of type 2 diabetes.

nodes.label: Filtered glucose
nodes.info: Glucose filtered by the kidney. When blood glucose is normal the proximal tubule reclaims nearly all of it.

nodes.label: Reabsorbed to blood
nodes.info: Glucose taken back from the tubule into the blood by SGLT2 (mostly) and SGLT1.

nodes.label: Lost in urine
nodes.info: What SGLT2 does not reclaim leaves in the urine. This is how SGLT2 inhibitors lower blood glucose, independent of insulin.

edges.info: Glucose absorbed from the meal in the small intestine. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose, miglitol) delay the breakdown of starch to glucose, so absorption is slower and the rise after a meal is smaller.
edges.label: gut absorption
liver output
edges.info: Glucose output by the liver. Metformin lowers it (mainly by reducing gluconeogenesis); incretin-based drugs lower glucagon and so lower it too.

edges.label: beta cell
edges.info: Insulin release by the beta cell in response to glucose. Sulfonylureas close K-ATP channels, depolarise the cell and release insulin whatever the glucose (so hypoglycaemia is possible); DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists raise release in a glucose-dependent way.

edges.label: insulin · GLUT4
edges.info: Insulin action on muscle and fat. Thiazolidinediones act on PPAR-gamma, mainly in fat, and raise insulin sensitivity over weeks; metformin raises it a little.

edges.label: SGLT2
edges.info: The sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT2 of the proximal tubule reclaims most filtered glucose. An SGLT2 inhibitor blocks it, so more glucose is lost in the urine, independent of insulin.
Reclaimed glucose returning to the blood.
Filtered glucose that is not reclaimed.

sources: Sulfonylureas and thiazolidinediones. Sulfonylureas bind the sulfonylurea receptor 1 of the K-ATP channel on beta cells, close it, depolarise the cell, open calcium channels and trigger insulin release whatever the glucose, which is why hypoglycaemia occurs; thiazolidinediones activate PPAR-gamma, mainly in fat, raising insulin sensitivity over weeks (Oral antidiabetic medications, StatPearls).

Metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors. Metformin mainly reduces hepatic glucose output and to a lesser extent raises insulin sensitivity; SGLT2 inhibitors block renal glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule, an effect independent of insulin and so less likely to cause hypoglycaemia (Oral hypoglycemic drugs: pathophysiological basis of their mechanism of action, PMC; Oral agents in type 2 diabetes, AAFP).

Incretin-based drugs. DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists raise glucose-dependent insulin release and lower glucagon; this is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and was not checked against a linked source here, so it is flagged for review.
simplified: Insulin itself (and its types) is shown only as the natural signal: injected insulin acts at the same uptake step, with hypoglycaemia as its main risk. Not drawn: glucagon, fat and muscle effects on weight, alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, meglitinides, amylin analogues, the feedback of glucose on insulin release, lactate, ketones, kidney threshold effects, heart and kidney outcomes, genital infection and volume effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, and the slow onset of thiazolidinediones. The blood glucose level is a teaching score, not a measured value. Levels, flow and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors and meglitinides are shown as simple options: delayed absorption and a quick, short insulin release.
